summary:
Siirt province stands under the national framework of Turkey, and no Siirt-specific ban, enforcement programme, incident or local institution concerning transgender visitors is documented in the audited sources. What a trans visitor to Siirt faces is the country-wide regime, applied by national ministries, provincial governors and police stations that operate the same powers throughout the country.

That regime is actively tightening. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, carrying up to three years' imprisonment, with participation in same-sex ceremonies punishable by up to four years. The same package would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from eighteen to twenty-five, attach mandatory infertility conditions and multi-stage evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers of such care for up to seven years and patients for up to three. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object to the measures.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report for 2025/26 records that three draft law packages targeting LGBT people were made public during 2025, seeking to criminalise LGBT identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and to make legal gender recognition nearly impossible. None was ultimately submitted to parliament. A related proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging behaviour contrary to biological sex, carrying a one-to-three-year sentence, was also omitted from the 12th judicial package. The pattern across these drafts is of measures announced and enforced in substance before, or without, enactment.

The settled law remains comparatively old. Homosexuality was decriminalised under the Ottoman penal code in 1858 and legal gender change has been available in Turkey since 1988. Same-sex marriage is not recognised, and LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military.

Pride events are prohibited rather than merely policed. Governors blocked the Istanbul parades held between 2015 and 2018, and on 14 June 2019 the governors of Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya banned all three cities' prides. In June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches; police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at the end of the year.

Civil society faces closure. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had circulated images incompatible with society's moral values.
tangentialFactors:
The parent framework documented for Turkey includes street-level controls that reach every province. Police stop people for background checks and hold them at stations for documentation, and foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at checkpoints with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. For a trans visitor in Siirt, any such stop is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation.

National monitoring recorded 313 violations of LGBTI+ rights in a single year, roughly two and a half times the previous year's total, alongside 299 detention decisions. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence over that period, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected.

Prison conditions form a separate strand of the same pattern. Trans prisoners in Turkey are placed according to registered sex rather than gender identity, and reports of arbitrary body and strip searches, isolation with restricted healthcare access, and ineffective complaints mechanisms indicate that a trans person who is detained anywhere in the country, including in Siirt, enters a system administered on a binary basis.

Transition-related care is also narrowing. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, barred hospitals from recording an 'other' option in medical-board reports and required electronic reports, a change framed by rights monitors as risking the profiling of trans patients in official records.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition has been available in Turkey since 1988, but the pending judicial packages would remove civil-status recognition of gender change and impose infertility conditions on those who seek it, so residents currently navigating that process face a framework under active threat of curtailment.

Residents cannot marry a same-sex partner, and open service in the military is barred for LGBTQ personnel.

Local organisers operate under the risk of association closure and prosecution. The December 2025 dissolution order against the Young LGBTI+ Association in İzmir establishes that courts will dissolve an LGBTI+ organisation over content deemed incompatible with prevailing moral standards, and the 92 ongoing pride prosecutions show that participation in banned marches carries a live criminal case.

Detained residents are placed in facilities according to registered sex, with documented reports of a trans man held in a women's prison, delayed medical response, and custody conditions for trans prisoners under formal contestation in parliament by the end of 2025.

Access to transition-related care depends on medical-board reporting that has been narrowed by the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, which removed the 'other' option and moved reports onto electronic systems.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Siirt-specific incident, arrest, local ordinance, hospital practice or police directive concerning transgender people is sourced here; the province is described only by the national framework that applies to it, and any Siirt-level enforcement record remains unresolved.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package and the other draft packages reported in 2025 have since been introduced to parliament, amended or abandoned is not sourced in this inventory; only their published terms and their non-submission during 2025 are recorded.

The status of the proposal to criminalise publicly encouraging behaviour contrary to biological sex after its omission from the 12th judicial package is unresolved.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri circular are applied by hospitals in Siirt, and how gender-recognition applications from Siirt are currently processed, is not sourced.

The number of prosecutions arising from pride bans in 2025 and their outcomes at trial, beyond the figure of 92 cases continuing at year's end, is not documented in this inventory.
